extracted.intended_audience: independent inventors, pro se patent applicants, and patent practitioners seeking to understand 35 U.S.C. §102/§103 rejections in an office action
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how examiners establish and applicants respond to rejections under 35 U.S.C. §§102 and 103 (anticipation and obviousness), including what counts as prior art, evidence types, prima facie burdens, and the factual inquiries from Graham/KSR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of patentability and prima facie burden
rubrics_metrics.description: Claimed inventions are presumed to be patentable unless the examiner is able to establish a prima facie case that one of the patentability requirements is not met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A prima facie case is one that at first sight presents sufficient evidence to support the conclusion. An examiner's evidence is prior art (e.g., publications, patents, admissions, on-sale items). Anticipation (35 U.S.C. §102) and obviousness (35 U.S.C. §103) are most frequent. If examiner establishes prima facie case, burden shifts to applicant to rebut or supply evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation under 35 U.S.C. §102 (single-reference test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipation occurs when a single prior art reference describes, either expressly or inherently, each and every limitation of a claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single prior art reference anticipates the claimed invention by describing every limitation in the claim; limitations can be expressly set forth or inherently present in the reference. If conditions of §102(a)(1) are met, claims lack novelty and should be rejected under §102(a)(1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of evidence to support prior art rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art rejections may rely on several types of evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence types include: (1) References — printed documents including patents and non-patent literature (see MPEP 2126-2128); (2) Admissions — applicant statements admitting prior art (MPEP 2129); (3) Affidavits/declarations — sworn evidentiary statements showing knowledge/activity; (4) Knowledge in the art — logical reasoning or common knowledge, sometimes by official notice (MPEP 2144).

rubrics_metrics.name: AIA FITF 'otherwise available to the public' (expanded prior art)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the America Invents Act First-Inventor-To-File, prior art includes things 'otherwise available to the public.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include oral presentations at scientific meetings, demonstrations at trade shows, lectures/speeches, radio statements, YouTube videos, websites, or other online material. This is a catch-all category under 35 U.S.C. §102(a)(1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory categories of §102(a)(1) prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: §102(a)(1) enumerates categories of prior art that negate novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statute states: (1) the claimed invention was patented, described in a printed publication, or (2) in public use, on sale, or otherwise available to the public before the effective filing date. Examiners determine these conditions after a complete search.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete search and novelty determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty determination under §102(a)(1) is made after a complete search for the claimed invention is done.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the conditions are met (novelty lacking), reject claims under §102(a)(1). If not, no §102(a)(1) rejection is made, but other statutes (e.g., §101, §102(a)(2), §103, §112) may still apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-obviousness under 35 U.S.C. §103 (statutory standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed invention is unpatentable under §103 if differences between the claimed invention and the prior art are such that the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious to a person having ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentability shall not be negated by the manner in which the invention was made. See MPEP 2141.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to employ a §103 rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Use §103 when the claimed invention is not identically disclosed in prior art and the reference teachings must be modified to meet the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The differences must have been obvious before the effective filing date and to a person having ordinary skill in the art; see MPEP 706.02.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham v. John Deere factual inquiries (framework for obviousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Four factual inquiries must be addressed to determine obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1) Scope and content of the prior art; 2) Differences between the prior art and the claims at issue; 3) Relevant level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art; 4) Any objective evidence of non-obviousness. See MPEP 2141; KSR affirmed continued use of this framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inquiry: scope and content of the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine what the prior art teaches and its content and scope as the first step in obviousness analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP 2141.01. This includes assessing specialized technical disclosures and common understanding available pre-filing date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art for §103 includes both technical and common knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art for obviousness purposes comprises specialized understanding of one of ordinary skill and common understanding of the layman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most §103 rejections are based on references available under §102. In addition to §102 references, examiners may rely on official notice, common sense, common ingenuity, and obvious matters of design choice provided sufficient explanation is set forth to establish a prima facie case (see MPEP 2143-2144).

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining references to support a §103 rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: A 103 rejection may be based on a combination of multiple references rather than a single reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must be cautious when combining elements from prior art (KSR). Rationale may include interrelated teachings of multiple patents, marketplace demands, known design constraints, and the background knowledge of a person of ordinary skill. The examiner must articulate why the combination would have been made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima facie obviousness — examiner's initial burden
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner must establish a prima facie case that the claimed invention would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the pertinent art before the effective filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner must supply facts and reasoning supporting a prima facie conclusion of obviousness (see MPEP 2142-2144). Mere conclusory statements are inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden shifts to applicant only after prima facie established
rubrics_metrics.description: If the examiner establishes a prima facie case of obviousness, the applicant bears the burden of presenting evidence or arguments of non-obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant evidence may include comparative test data showing improved properties not expected in view of the prior art. If the examiner fails to establish a prima facie case, the applicant need not provide such evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person of ordinary skill in the art (POSITA) perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness must be assessed from the viewpoint of a hypothetical person of ordinary skill in the art as of just before the effective filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner must 'step backward in time' and consider how that person would view the claimed invention given the state of the art at that time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the claimed invention 'as a whole'
rubrics_metrics.description: The determination of obviousness must evaluate the claimed invention in its entirety rather than piecemeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taking into account all factual information, the examiner must determine whether the claimed invention 'as a whole' would have been obvious to POSITA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Articulation of rationale — required reasoning underlying 103 rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: A clear articulation of the rationale or reasons why the claimed invention would have been obvious is essential to support a §103 rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mere conclusory statements are inadequate; there must be some articulated reasoning with rational underpinning to support the legal conclusion of obviousness (In re Kahn). If the office action does not explain WHY the combination or modification would have been made, the examiner has failed to set forth necessary rationale and cannot shift the burden to applicant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preponderance of evidence standard in patentability determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentability decisions are based on a preponderance of evidence (>50% likelihood).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If examiner determines there is factual support for an obviousness rejection, the examiner must consider all evidence supporting patentability, including specification disclosures and applicant-submitted evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on modifications of prior art (operability and principle of operation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A prima facie case of obviousness cannot be established if the proposed modification of a prior art invention would render it inoperable/unsatisfactory or would change its principle of operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If modification would make the prior art inoperative or alter its operating principle, there is no reason to make the modification and prima facie obviousness fails (see MPEP 2143.01).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable expectation of success requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness requires a reasonable expectation of success in making the claimed invention from the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some degree of predictability is required, though not absolute predictability. See MPEP 2143.02.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of all claim limitations when asserting obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: All claim limitations must be considered when establishing a prima facie case of obviousness, including indefinite limitations and limitations lacking specification support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "All words in a claim must be considered in judging the patentability of that claim against the prior art" (In re Wilson). See MPEP 2143.03.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against impermissible hindsight
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiner must not use the application's disclosure against the claims (except admissions of prior art) to show obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With the exception of admissions, the disclosure of the application being examined cannot be used to negate patentability, though examiner can use applicant's statements about state of the art and known problems in the art.
